title: The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 19 – The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas
explanation: Today’s image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt . The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse’s head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula . It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula . Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this "painting" were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories , but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois .

title: A Medium-Sized Solar Flare
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 18 – A Medium-Sized Solar Flare
explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . title: Milky Way versus Aurora
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 17 – Milky Way versus Aurora
explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our Milky Way Galaxy , an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates our Earth and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an auroral ribbon that is only hours old, composed of energized atoms and molecules , and is close by — right in Earth’s upper atmosphere . These chance-superposed titan s have our Sun in common, a stellar member of the Milky Way that ejects energetic particles which create aurora s. Far behind the middle of the auroral arch is the Big Dipper . Even farther in the distance is the Andromeda galaxy — the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The featured image was taken about a month ago from Kvaløya in northern Norway . title: NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb
explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when. Tomorrow’s picture: sky duel Date: November 16, 2

title: Leonid Meteors Through Orion
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 15 – Leonid Meteors Through Orion
explanation: Where will the next meteor appear? Even during a meteor shower, it is practically impossible to know. Therefore, a good way to enjoy a meteor shower is to find a place where you can sit comfortably and monitor a great expanse of dark sky. And it may be satisfying to share this experience with a friend. The meteor shower depicted was the 2022 Leonids and the view is from Hainan , China looking out over the South China Sea . Meteor streaks captured over a few hours were isolated and added to a foreground image recorded earlier. Leonid meteor streaks trace back to the constellation of Leo and were here seen streaking across the constellation of Orion. The bright red planet Mars appears near the top of the image. The Leonids peak in mid-November every year and so will peak again this week. Bonding over their love of astronomy, the two pictured meteor enthusiasts, shown celebrating their common birthday this month, were later married. Tomorr

title: Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3
explanation: Put on your red/blue glasses and gaze across the western Ocean of Storms on the surface of the Moon. The 3D anaglyph shows Apollo 12 astronaut Pete Conrad visiting the Surveyor 3 spacecraft in November of 1969. Surveyor 3 had landed at the site on the inside slope of a small crater about 2 1/2 years earlier in April of 1967. Visible on the horizon beyond the far crater wall, Apollo 12’s Lunar Module Intrepid touched down less than 200 meters (650 feet) away, easy moonwalking distance from the robotic Surveyor spacecraft. This stereo image was carefully created from two separate pictures ( AS12-48-7133 , AS12-48-7134 ) captured on the lunar surface . They depict the scene from only slightly different viewpoints, approximating the separation between human eyes. Tomorrow’s picture: meteors through Orion Date: November 14, 2026 Credit: Apollo 12 , Alan Bean – Stereo Image Copyright: Kevin Frank Authors & editors: Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chir

title: NGC 206 and the Star Clouds of Andromeda
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 13 – NGC 206 and the Star Clouds of Andromeda
explanation: The large stellar association cataloged as NGC 206 is nestled within the dusty arms of the neighboring Andromeda galaxy along with the galaxy’s pinkish star-forming regions. Also known as M31, the spiral galaxy is a mere 2.5 million light-years away. NGC 206 is found at the center of this sharp and detailed close-up of the southwestern extent of Andromeda’s disk. The bright, blue stars of NGC 206 indicate its youth. In fact, its youngest massive stars are less than 10 million years old. Much larger than the open or galactic clusters of young stars in the disk of our Milky Way galaxy, NGC 206 spans about 4,000 light-years. That’s comparable in size to the giant stellar nurseries NGC 604 in nearby spiral M33 and the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud. title: Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 12 – Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
explanation: Not all those who wander are lost. A night sky example is that planets wander, and in fact the very word "planet" comes from "wandering star" in Greek. As planets shift relative to fixed stars , they may appear from our perspective to get closer to other astronomical objects. Such meetings are called conjunctions . They don’t happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of celestial mechanics . This peaceful image , captured in Poland , shows the crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains , and bright Venus close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo , the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that Spica is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a triple system

title: NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 11 – NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact
explanation: Don’t judge a galaxy by its size. Our home galaxy, the Milky Way , is about 100,000 light years across. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called dwarf galaxies , are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the most common type of galaxy in the whole universe. Today’s image shows one such dwarf galaxy, NGC 4449 , captured by the Hubble Space Telescope . NGC 4449 and similar dwarf galaxies are missing more oxygen than models predict. This suggests their stellar winds and supernovae are surprisingly effective at blowing away oxygen and other heavy elements. Turns out these tiny galaxies may play a big role in spreading heavy elements — the building blocks of stars, planets, and life — throughout the universe! Tomorrow’s picture: a date in Poland Date: November 11, 2026 Credit: NASA, ESA, A. Aloisi (STScI/ESA), and the Hubble Heritage

title: Saturn Behind the Moon
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 10 – Saturn Behind the Moon
explanation: Sometimes Saturn disappears. It doesn’t really go away, of course — it just disappears from our view when Earth’s Moon moves in front. Such a Saturn ian eclipse, more formally called an occultation , was visible in early 2025 along a small swath of Earth — from Greenland through central Europe and into northern Africa . The featured image is a digital fusion of three images, the first of just Saturn before it disappeared, and then two more of the Moon with different exposure lengths. The images were taken from Sardinia , Italy , after sunset. The bright dot near Saturn is not a moon of Saturn , but rather the star 85 Aquarii , which is further behind Saturn than Saturn is behind the Moon. The next time the Moon moves in front of Saturn, as visible from some place on Earth , will be in 2031. title: Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 9 – Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula
explanation: Does the blue nebula look like the head of a witch? The nebula is known popularly as the Witch Head Nebula because, it is said, the nebula’s shape resembles a Halloween-style caricature of a witch’s head. Exactly how, though, can be a topic of imaginative speculation . What is clear is that IC 2118 is about 50 light-years across and made of gas and dust that points to — because it has been partly eroded by — the nearby star Rigel . One of the brighter stars in the constellation Orion, Rigel lies just below the center of the featured image . The blue color of the Witch Head Nebula and is caused not only by Rigel’s intense blue starlight but also because the dust grains scatter blue light more efficiently than red. The same physical process causes Earth’s daytime sky to appear blue , although the scatterers in planet Earth’s atmosphere are molecules of nitrogen and oxygen . Tomorrow’s picture: suddenly Saturn Date: November 9, 2026 Credit

title: Major Fireball Meteor
explanation: The sky glows with soft pinkish colors of fading twilight in this serendipitous mountaintop vista. Taken in subfreezing temperatures, the thoughtfully composed photo shows snowy, rugged peaks seen from a mountain pass on 2017 November 14. Below lies the village of La Villa, Alta Badia in Italy ’s Dolomite Alps . Above the nestled village lights, the constellation Ursa Major hangs over the northern horizon. But most stunning is the intense fireball meteor. It was captured during the camera’s exposure by chance as it flashed east to west across the northern horizon, under Ursa Major’s familiar Big Dipper asterism . Sightings of this major fireball meteor were widely reported in European skies, making it one of the most reported fireball events ever for planet Earth’s American Meteor Society and the International Meteor Organization . The meteor’s measured track over Germany is consistent with its origin near the active radiant of November

title: De Gerlache-Kocher Massif
explanation: De Gerlache-Kocher massif looms on the visible horizon in this close-up of the edge of the Moon. The mountainous formation rises about 4 kilometers above its surroundings and is located very close to the lunar south pole. Boasting permanently shadowed crater floors that likely contain deposits of water ice and peaks that receive almost continuous sunlight for solar power generation, the south polar region is considered a prime location for the first human settlement on the Moon. In fact , De Gerlache-Kocher massif itself has been considered as a potential landing site for future crewed Artemis missions to the Moon . The remarkable telescopic image of the massif at the lunar limb was captured on October 31. Then, a favorable libration angle or lunar wobble enhanced this oblique view across the Moon’s south pole. Tomorrow’s picture: meteoric Date: November 7, 2026 Credit: Alejandro Sanz Authors & editors: Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti,

title: A Farewell to Swift
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 6 – A Farewell to Swift
explanation: It is time to say goodbye to NASA ’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory . After nearly 22 years of service, the satellite re-entered Earth’s atmosphere on November 4 at 7:39 EST over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia . The featured image is a mosaic created in 2018 using some of the first million images captured by the satellite’s Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope . Swift had a combination of instruments, including an X-ray telescope and a gamma-ray telescope , that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energetic explosions in the universe. The most recent solar maximum accelerated the decay of the satellite’s orbit. An innovative mission to rescue Swift by boosting its orbit was not successful . Swift burned on reentry like a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May

title: Enceladus in Silhouette
explanation: One of our Solar System’s most tantalizing worlds, Enceladus is backlit by the Sun in this Cassini spacecraft image from November 1, 2009. The dramatic illumination reveals the plumes that continuously spew into space from the south pole of Saturn’s 500 kilometer diameter moon . Discovered by Cassini in 2005, the icy plumes are likely connected to an ocean beneath the ice shell of Enceladus. They supply material directly to Saturn’s outer, tenuous E ring and make the surface of Enceladus as reflective as snow. Across the scene, Saturn’s icy rings scatter sunlight toward Cassini’s cameras. Beyond the rings (lower right), the night side of 80 kilometer diameter moon Pandora is faintly lit by Saturnlight . title: The Not-So-Hidden Galaxy, IC 342
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 4 – The Not-So-Hidden Galaxy, IC 342
explanation: “I see” IC 342, the Hidden Galaxy! Today’s image peers through the plane of the Milky Way , through all its gas, dust and stars, to unveil this spiral galaxy . IC 342 (or Caldwell 5 ) is one of the brightest members of the IC 342/ Maffei group of galaxies. Located about 10 million light years away, this group is quite close to the Local Group that includes our Milky Way. Inaccurate accounting of the crowded and dusty Milky Way foreground has led to misunderstandings in IC 342’s history, including the theory that the galaxy was ejected from the Local Group . IC 342 has its own dust intermittently blocking the glow of hydrogen gas , indicating the presence of bright, young stars. Magnetic field maps of IC 342 reveal that magnetic fields may contribute substantially to one of the biggest galactic puzzles: how do spiral arms form ? Tomorrow’s picture: open space Date: November 4, 2026 Credit & Copyright: Artem Mironov Authors & editors: Kei

title: Comet PanSTARRs and Rainbow Meteor
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 3 – Comet PanSTARRs and Rainbow Meteor
explanation: Did this meteor come from that comet? Probably not. Although many meteors do originate from comets, there are thousands of comets that have visited the inner Solar System recently, and matching meteors to them can be tricky. And to be clear, the pictured comet is far behind the streaking meteor . Comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) was captured from Hautacam , France in April when the giant space iceberg sported impressive ion (blue) and dust tails . Sand-sized rocky debris that enters Earth’s atmosphere typically appears as meteors , while the colorful foreground streak here may indicate a complicated composition. This month three notable meteor showers will reach their peaks. Over the next few days, the Southern Taurids will be reaching their apex, while the Northern Taurids will top out about a week later. Both originate from Comet 2P/Encke . November is most famous for the Leonids Meteor Shower , though, which originates from Comet 55P/Temp

title: A Long Cloud on Mars
fullHeading: APOD: 2026 November 2 – A Long Cloud on Mars
explanation: What’s causing this unusually long cloud on Mars ? Known as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) and first recorded by NASA’s Viking Orbiter 2 in 1977, the strange cloud has been imaged in greater detail more recently by ESA ’s robotic Mars Express spacecraft. The featured image is from 2018. The cloud forms only during spring and summer seasons and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes cloud crystals to form around bits of dust would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the Martian atmosphere . Leading speculation holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons , wind blows the cloud downstream — creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand AMEC s will continue, an understanding that may bolster a more complete view of cloud formation on Earth . Tomorrow’s picture: eyeing a cat Date: November 2, 2026
